_comment: The estate's own work orders: what the fabricator builds that is not an
application. Each names the image it publishes (ghcr.io/<repository>-<name>)
and the directory holding its Dockerfile, which is also the build context.
An application is not written here. One that has an image is an order by
being there: named for its directory under modules/applications/, built
from image/ inside it, and released as its application.json says.
.github/workflows/fabricator.yml composes the two lists and builds every
order in the result, and nothing else: it does not look for work.
Completeness is checked by a guard, not by the fabricator:
tests/go/repo/fabricator_test.go walks the repository and fails on a
Dockerfile with no order, and on an order whose Dockerfile is gone.
An order may instead publish a package: a set of the repository's own files,
named by a manifest, published whole under a version as
ghcr.io/<repository>-<name>-release. The platform is one - the modules a site
runs and what they read - and a site runs the version its own config pins,
so merging a change to it does nothing to production. The version is the
year and month it was published in and its number within that month.
An image's build sees its own directory and nothing else of the repository,
unless the order says what else it reads. Those files are handed to the
build as a second context named reads, laid out by their paths here, and
they are part of the image's fingerprint: a change to one is a new image.
The pull-request runner reads the locked installer and its lock, so that
what it carries arrived by the same hashes as on every other machine.
